You pass if you found both copies, counted no copy at either

Data flow through a pipeline is a chain of stages handing a buffer to the next, and it is correct exactly when every buffer has an owner, the object whose destructor frees it, at every moment, and every other user finishes before that owner goes away. There are four ways to hand a buffer onward. A copy gives the next stage an owner of its own, at a cost of size times rate. A move hands ownership over and leaves the source valid but unspecified, never to be read again. Sharing, through a
, fits two consumers that both need the data with neither sure which finishes last, because the last owner frees it. A borrow, through a
, uses the data without owning it, safe for the length of the call and nothing longer.

The problem this solves is copying nobody asked for. A stage taking and returning its argument by value copies a buffer at every boundary, because an lvalue can't be moved from without saying so, and for a 2.76 MB camera frame at 30 Hz that is real bandwidth spent before any actual work happens. The other half is rate: a producer faster than its consumer grows a queue by the difference every second, and no queue size fixes a rate mismatch alone.
The mechanism is naming, at each line, who owns the buffer right now, and choosing the cheapest handoff that keeps that answer true.

moves a value through every step because none of it is bound to a named variable, so nothing is copied. A bounded queue makes the rate problem explicit the same way: block the producer, drop the oldest item, or refuse the new one, but always count what is dropped.

What it costs, at the failure end, is silence. An unbounded queue fails slowly: every item still gets processed, only later and later, so a short test passes and the system runs out of memory an hour into a real shift. A borrow stored past the call it arrived in fails the same way any dangling reference does, reading memory its owner already freed.

You meet this in the interview question itself: say which lines copy a message's data as it crosses three pipeline stages, how many bytes a second that costs, and who owns it after each line, then rewrite the pipeline so nothing copies.

c.v: The code of the three versions is almost the same, and the cost is not. Passing by value copies each frame twice, 16,588,800 bytes for three frames. At 30 Hz that is 166 MB of copying a second, as much as the two raw cameras in the requirements topic's exercise send to disk. Moving copies nothing, and neither does sharing.
Each version answers one question for every buffer: who owns it? The

is the object whose destructor frees the buffer, and a data flow is correct when every buffer has an owner at every moment and every other user is done before the owner goes away. There are four ways to hand data to the next stage:

items.v: A copy gives the next stage an owner of its own. It is the simplest to get right, and its cost is size times rate. For a 16-byte odometry sample it is nothing; for a camera frame it dominates.

A move hands ownership over and leaves the pixels where they are. The buffer belongs to the destination afterwards, and the source is left valid but unspecified, as the copy and move topic showed: the producer may still destroy it, assign a new frame to it or ask a container whether it is empty, and it must not read the value it held. Treating a moved-from input as gone is the rule you want for a pipeline stage anyway. An empty source is guaranteed only where the type promises it: a moved-from
. A function that takes ownership says so in its signature, with a by-value parameter or a
, fits fan-out: a recorder and a viewer both need the frame, and neither knows which finishes last. The last owner frees it. The
matters: data shared between stages, and so between threads, must not change while others read it (
). The price is a reference count that every copy of the pointer updates atomically.
, uses the data without owning it. It is the right parameter type for a stage that only reads (
), and it is safe for exactly as long as the call. Stored in a member or a queue, a borrow outlives the call, and nothing ties it to the owner's lifetime. Abseil's
puts it as views being safe as parameters and risky when stored.

c.v: prefers passing small data between threads by value, because a copy has no lifetime to get wrong. The decision is a number, size times rate: moving a 16-byte odometry sample saves nothing, and copying camera frames costs 166 MB a second.

The second half of a data flow is rates. Every queue has a producer and a consumer, and each has a rate. When the producer is faster, the queue grows by the difference: a camera at 30 Hz and a recorder at 25 Hz add 5 frames, 13.8 MB, to the queue every second, with no end. No queue size fixes a rate mismatch. Only three things do: make the consumer faster, slow the producer down, or drop data on purpose.
makes that choice explicit, because it has to decide what happens when it is full:

items.v: Block the producer until there is room. The consumer's pace then pushes back up the pipeline, which is
. It fits a producer that can wait, such as a file converter, and not a camera, which can't pause the scene.
Drop the oldest item. The queue always holds the newest data, which fits sensor streams and control, where an old measurement is worth less than a new one.
Refuse the new item and tell the producer, which fits jobs and requests that someone must retry or report.

c.v: Whichever you choose, count the drops, or the loss is invisible. The size of the bound comes from the requirements: the longest stall to survive times the data rate. The logger in the requirements topic buffers 2 s at 93 KB/s, 186 KB, and drops the oldest data when a stall lasts longer. The memory bound of a pipeline is then the sum over its queues of capacity times item size, plus the items each stage holds while it works.
ROS 2 has the same pieces. A subscription's history depth is a bounded queue that keeps the newest messages: with
and depth 10, the eleventh unread message pushes out the oldest (

). Between processes, with the default settings, the publisher serializes each message into the middleware's format and each subscriber deserializes it into its own message, so every hop costs at least a copy on each side. Within one process, with
, a single subscriber receives the publisher's own buffer with no copy. With two such subscribers, one gets the original and the other a copy. The

The bound caps the memory at 5 frames, 13,824,000 bytes, and it makes the loss explicit: 5 frames dropped and counted, where the unbounded version hid a queue that never stops growing. It doesn't make the recorder faster. At 30 frames in and 25 out, any bound fills, and from then on 5 frames a second are dropped. That is a requirement to settle rather than a bug to fix: record at 25 Hz by design and skip every sixth frame on purpose, or make the recorder keep up, for example by compressing, as in the requirements topic's camera exercise.

subs.title: Unbounded buffers; borrowing past the owner

c.v: An unbounded queue fails slowly. This program runs the camera and the recorder from the exercise for 60 s, queueing only the stamps and computing the pixel memory they stand for:

blocks.text:
no bound  recorded 1500, dropped 0, queue peak 300 frames = 829440000 bytes
bound 30  recorded 1500, dropped 270, queue peak 30 frames = 82944000 bytes

c.v: Without a bound, the queue holds 829 MB after one minute and keeps growing by 13.8 MB a second until the process runs out of memory. Nothing fails before that: every frame is still recorded, only later and later, so a short test passes, and the robot falls over an hour into a shift. With a bound of 30 frames, 1 s of camera, the memory stays at 83 MB and the same mismatch shows up as 270 counted drops, which a test and an operator can see. Both versions record the same 1500 frames, because the recorder's rate decides that. The bound only decides what the other 300 cost.
Unbounded queues hide in ordinary code: a
member that a callback appends to, a ROS subscription with

history, which is limited only by the middleware's resource limits, a logger's memory buffer, or a thread pool's task list. For each one, write down its producer, its consumer, both rates and its bound.
